# 6.5 - Permutations {.unnumbered}

A club of 10 students picks a president, a vice president, and a secretary. How many different ways can they fill the three jobs?

Listing them all would take a long time. There are 720 ways. In this lesson, you learn to count arrangements without listing them.

:::{.objectives}
- [ ] I use the counting principle.
- [ ] I find and use factorials.
- [ ] I count permutations with ${}_nP_r$.
- [ ] I decide if repeats are allowed.
:::

### 6.5.1 - The Counting Principle

:::{.remember title="The Counting Principle"}
If one choice has $m$ options and a second choice has $n$ options, there are $m \cdot n$ ways to make both choices.
:::

**Example:** 3 shirts and 4 pairs of pants make $3 \cdot 4 = 12$ outfits.

***

### 6.5.2 - Factorials

In how many ways can 4 students sit in 4 chairs in a row?

| Chair 1 | Chair 2 | Chair 3 | Chair 4 |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 4 choices | 3 left | 2 left | 1 left |

$$
4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 24 \text{ ways}
$$

:::{.remember title="Factorial"}
$$
n! = n \cdot (n - 1) \cdot (n - 2) \cdots 2 \cdot 1
$$

Read $n!$ as "$n$ factorial." For example, $4! = 24$ and $1! = 1$.

Also, $0! = 1$. There is exactly one way to arrange nothing.
:::

***

### 6.5.3 - Permutations

A {{< glink permutation >}} is an arrangement where **order matters**.

In the club example, Ana as president and Ben as vice president is different from Ben as president and Ana as vice president. So order matters: $10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 = 720$ ways.

:::{.remember title="The Permutation Formula"}
$$
{}_nP_r = \frac{n!}{(n - r)!}
$$

This counts the ways to arrange $r$ things chosen from $n$ things. Read ${}_nP_r$ as "$n$ permute $r$." Some books write $P(n, r)$.
:::

$$
{}_{10}P_3 = \frac{10!}{7!} = \frac{10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8 \cdot \cancel{7 \cdot 6 \cdots 1}}{\cancel{7 \cdot 6 \cdots 1}} = 720
$$

:::{.gotcha title="Repeats allowed?"}
3-letter codes from 26 letters:

- **No repeats:** $26 \cdot 25 \cdot 24 = 15{,}600$. This is a permutation.
- **Repeats allowed:** $26 \cdot 26 \cdot 26 = 26^3 = 17{,}576$. This is not a permutation. Use the counting principle.
:::

:::{.you-try title="In how many ways can 5 people stand in a line?"}
$5! = 5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 1 = 120$
:::

{{< practice >}}

Work with a partner. Compare answers when you finish each problem.

**Factorials and Permutations**

1. Find each value.

   a. $5!$

   b. $\dfrac{6!}{4!}$

   c. $0!$

   d. ${}_8P_3$

2. You have 5 shirts, 3 pairs of pants, and 2 pairs of shoes. How many outfits can you make?

3. In how many ways can 6 different books be arranged on a shelf?

4. 8 runners are in a race. In how many ways can gold, silver, and bronze medals be given?

***

**Repeats and Reasoning**

5. A phone code has 4 digits (0 to 9).

   a. How many codes are there if digits can repeat?

   b. How many codes are there if no digit repeats?

6. In how many ways can you arrange the letters of the word MATH?

7. A club of 12 members picks a president and a treasurer. One person cannot have both jobs. How many ways?

8. Explain why ${}_{10}P_3$ is the same as $10 \cdot 9 \cdot 8$.
